lessons.title: Lesson 1: What deep learning is
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain deep learning in your own words and name where it is used.
This lesson builds toward: Without notes, you will explain what deep learning is and name the kinds of data it works best on, mentioning layers that learn patterns from examples and at least two fitting kinds of data.
Deep learning is a kind of machine learning that uses neural networks: many small math units, called neurons, joined in layers. "Deep" means there are many layers. Each layer finds patterns in the output of the one before it.
For a picture, early layers notice simple things like edges, middle layers notice shapes, and later layers notice whole objects like a face or a number. Nobody writes those rules: the network learns them from many labeled examples.
It works best when there is a lot of data and the data is messy and rich: images, sound, speech and long text. It needs more data and computing power than simpler models, which is why it took off once large datasets and fast graphics chips (GPUs) became common.
Words to know:
- Deep learning: machine learning with neural networks that have many layers.
- Neural network: a model made of many small units (neurons) joined in layers.
- Layer: a group of neurons that all take input from the layer before.
- GPU: a graphics chip that does many calculations at once, used to train networks fast.
Try it now: Write down four tools you have used that probably use deep learning (for example face unlock, voice typing, photo search, translation). For each, write what kind of data it learns from: images, sound or text.
You can now explain what deep learning is, why it uses layers, and where it is used.

check.q: What are neurons in a neural network?
options: Brain cells copied into a computer
Small math units joined in layers
check.why: A neural network is made of many small math units, called neurons, in layers.

check.q: Your unit wants to sort thousands of recorded radio messages by speaker. Would you consider deep learning?
options: Yes; it works best with a lot of rich data like sound
No; deep learning cannot use sound
No; it only works on numbers in a table
Only if there are fewer than ten recordings
check.why: Deep learning works best with lots of rich, messy data such as images, sound and text.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Inside a neuron: weights, bias and activation
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Work out by hand what a single neuron outputs.
This lesson builds toward: Given a neuron's inputs, weights, bias and ReLU, you will calculate the neuron's output by hand, getting the right answer every time, including when ReLU gives 0.
A neuron takes some numbers in, multiplies each by a weight, adds them up, and adds one more number called the bias. The weights say how important each input is; the network learns them.
Then it applies an activation function, which decides what to pass on. The most common one, ReLU, is simple: if the total is below zero, output 0; otherwise output the total.
Example: inputs 2 and 3, weights 0.5 and -1, bias 1. Total = 2 x 0.5 + 3 x (-1) + 1 = 1 - 3 + 1 = -1. ReLU turns -1 into 0, so this neuron outputs 0. With input 2 and 1 instead: 1 - 1 + 1 = 1, so it outputs 1.
A network has thousands of these. The last layer often uses softmax, which turns its outputs into chances that add up to 100 percent, one per possible answer.
Step by step:
- Multiply each input by its weight.
- Add the results together.
- Add the bias.
- Apply the activation: with ReLU, negative becomes 0.
- That number is the neuron's output.
Words to know:
- Neuron: a small unit that multiplies inputs by weights, adds a bias and applies an activation.
- Weight: a number the network learns that says how much an input matters.
- Bias: an extra number added to the total, also learned.
- Activation function: the rule that decides what a neuron passes on.
- ReLU: an activation: negative totals become 0, others stay the same.
- Softmax: turns the last layer's outputs into chances that add up to 1.
Try it now: Work out a neuron's output by hand: inputs 4 and 1, weights 0.5 and 2, bias -3, ReLU activation. Then change the bias to -6 and work it out again. (Answers: 1, then 0.)
You can now calculate a neuron's output from its inputs, weights, bias and activation.

check.q: In a neuron, what is the bias?
options: The input with the biggest value
A rule that says the model is unfair
One more number added after the weighted inputs are summed
check.why: The neuron adds the bias to the weighted sum before the activation.

check.q: Inputs 4 and 1, weights 0.5 and 2, bias -1, ReLU. What output would you calculate?
check.why: 4 x 0.5 + 1 x 2 - 1 = 3, and ReLU keeps positive totals.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: How a network learns: loss, epochs and small steps
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain how training changes the weights to make fewer mistakes.
This lesson builds toward: Given a training log with loss and accuracy, you will explain how training changes the weights and identify signs of overfitting, using the words loss, learning rate, epoch and validation correctly.
At the start, the weights are random, so the network's guesses are bad. Training fixes that. The network makes a guess, and a loss function measures how wrong it was: a big loss means very wrong, a small loss means close.
Then it works out, for every weight, which direction would lower the loss (this step is called backpropagation) and moves each weight a small step that way (gradient descent). The size of the step is the learning rate: too big and it overshoots, too small and it is very slow.
One pass through all the training examples is an epoch. Training usually takes several epochs. You watch the loss go down and accuracy go up, and you check a validation set (data held back from training) to catch overfitting: if training accuracy keeps rising but validation accuracy falls, stop.
Step by step:
- Start with random weights.
- Make guesses on training examples.
- Measure the error with the loss function.
- Nudge every weight a small step to lower the loss.
- Repeat for several epochs, watching validation accuracy.
Words to know:
- Loss: a number that measures how wrong the network's guesses are.
- Backpropagation: working out how each weight affected the loss.
- Gradient descent: moving the weights in small steps to lower the loss.
- Learning rate: how big each step is.
- Epoch: one full pass through the training data.
- Validation set: data held back during training to check for overfitting.
Try it now: Play "guess the number" with a friend or by yourself: pick a hidden number from 1 to 100, guess, get "too high" or "too low", and change your guess by a smaller step each time. Write down which part of the game is like the loss, which is like the learning rate, and how many rounds (epochs) it took.
You can now explain loss, backpropagation, gradient descent, learning rate, epochs and overfitting in plain words.

options: How many images are in the dataset
The size of each step the weights move
check.why: Too big a step overshoots; too small a step is very slow.

check.q: After epoch 4, validation accuracy starts to fall while training accuracy keeps rising. What would you do?
options: Stop training; the model is starting to overfit
Raise the learning rate a lot
check.why: Falling validation accuracy with rising training accuracy is a sign of overfitting.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Building a neural network in Colab

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Loading and preparing image data
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Load the MNIST digits in Colab, scale them, and look at one image.
This lesson builds toward: In Google Colab with Keras, you will load the MNIST digits, scale the pixels and display one image with its label, with pixels between 0 and 1 and the label matching the picture.
MNIST is a famous practice dataset: 70,000 small pictures of handwritten digits 0 to 9, each 28 by 28 pixels, with the right digit as the label. Keras, a free deep learning library that works in Google Colab, can load it with one line, already split into 60,000 training and 10,000 test images.
Each pixel is a number from 0 (black) to 255 (white). Networks learn better with small numbers, so you scale them to between 0 and 1 by dividing by 255. This is called normalizing.
Look at your data before training. matplotlib, a plotting library, can draw one image so you can check that the label matches the picture.
Step by step:
- In a new Colab notebook run: import keras
- Load: (x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test) = keras.datasets.mnist.load_data()
- Scale: x_train = x_train / 255.0 and x_test = x_test / 255.0
- Check sizes: print(x_train.shape, x_test.shape)
- Draw one: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt; plt.imshow(x_train[0], cmap="gray"); plt.show(); print(y_train[0])
Words to know:
- MNIST: a practice dataset of 70,000 handwritten digit images.
- Keras: a free, beginner-friendly Python library for building neural networks.
- Pixel: one dot of an image, stored as a number.
- Normalizing: scaling numbers to a small range like 0 to 1 so training works better.
- matplotlib: a Python library for drawing charts and images.
Official sources:
- Keras code example: Simple MNIST convnet
- Google Colab: Frequently Asked Questions
Try it now: Load and scale MNIST in Colab. Print the shapes of the training and test sets. Draw the images at positions 0, 1 and 2 and print their labels to check they match.
You can now load an image dataset, normalize it and check it by eye.

check.q: What does normalizing the MNIST pixels mean here?
options: Scaling them to between 0 and 1 by dividing by 255
check.why: Dividing by 255 turns 0 to 255 into 0 to 1, which helps learning.

check.q: You loaded MNIST and want to be sure the labels are right. What would you do?
options: Draw one image with matplotlib and check it matches its label
check.why: Look at your data before training to check the label matches the picture.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Building and training the network
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a Keras network, compile it and train it for a few epochs.
This lesson builds toward: Given the prepared MNIST data, you will build, compile and train a Keras neural network, with the code running, a validation split used and the loss going down across epochs.
A Sequential model is a stack of layers. Ours: keras.Input(shape=(28, 28)) says what goes in. layers.Flatten() turns each 28 x 28 picture into one row of 784 numbers. layers.Dense(128, activation="relu") is a layer of 128 neurons. layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax") is the output: one chance for each digit 0 to 9.
compile sets how it learns: optimizer="adam" (a popular kind of gradient descent), loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy" (the right loss when labels are plain numbers like 7), and metrics=["accuracy"] so you see how often it is right.
fit trains it: model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=5, validation_split=0.1). validation_split=0.1 holds back 10 percent of the training data to check for overfitting. Each epoch prints loss, accuracy, val_loss and val_accuracy. Watch the loss go down.
Step by step:
- from keras import layers
- model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input(shape=(28, 28)), layers.Flatten(), layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"), layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")])
- model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
- model.summary() to see the layers.
- model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=5, validation_split=0.1)
Words to know:
- Sequential model: a network made of layers stacked one after another.
- Flatten: a layer that turns a grid of pixels into one long row.
- Dense layer: a layer where every neuron connects to every input.
- Optimizer: the method that updates the weights; adam is a common one.
- compile: sets the optimizer, loss and metrics before training.
- validation_split: the share of training data held back to check for overfitting.
Official sources:
- Keras code example: Simple MNIST convnet
Try it now: Build, compile and train the network for 5 epochs. Write down the accuracy and val_accuracy after epoch 1 and after epoch 5. Did both go up?
You can now build a neural network in Keras, compile it and train it while watching for overfitting.

check.q: What is a Sequential model in Keras?
options: A stack of layers, one after another
check.why: Sequential stacks layers in order from input to output.

check.q: You want to see during training whether the model starts to overfit. What would you add to fit?
check.why: validation_split holds back some training data to check the model each epoch.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Testing, predicting and improving
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Measure test accuracy, predict real images, try one improvement and name the model's limits.
This lesson builds toward: Given a trained network, you will measure its test accuracy, predict new images, test one change and describe its limits, changing one thing at a time and naming at least one real limit.
The true test is data the network never saw: model.evaluate(x_test, y_test) prints the test loss and accuracy. A small network like ours usually gets well above 90 percent on MNIST.
To predict, give it images: probs = model.predict(x_test[:5]) gives 10 chances for each image. probs.argmax(axis=1) picks the digit with the highest chance. Compare those with y_test[:5].
To improve it, change one thing at a time and retest: more neurons (Dense(256)), more epochs, or a convolutional network (layers that scan small patches of the image), which reaches about 99 percent in the official Keras example.
Know the limits: it only knows centered, single digits like MNIST. A photo of a street sign or a letter will still get a digit. In real work, such as reading forms or inspecting parts, a person checks low-confidence results, and the model is tested on data from the real place it will be used.
Step by step:
- Run model.evaluate(x_test, y_test) and note the test accuracy.
- probs = model.predict(x_test[:5])
- print(probs.argmax(axis=1), y_test[:5]) to compare guesses with the truth.
- Change one thing (neurons or epochs), rebuild, retrain and re-evaluate.
- Write whether it helped and one limit.
Words to know:
- evaluate: tests the trained model on data and reports loss and accuracy.
- argmax: picks the position of the biggest number: here, the most likely digit.
- Convolutional network (CNN): a network with layers that scan small patches of an image; very good at pictures.
- Hyperparameter: a setting you choose, like neurons or epochs, rather than one the network learns.
Official sources:
- Keras code example: Simple MNIST convnet
Try it now: Final task: evaluate your network on the test set, predict the first five test images and compare with the true labels, then change Dense(128) to Dense(256) or epochs to 10, retrain and re-evaluate. Write two sentences: did the change help, and what is one limit of this model?
You can now train, test, use and improve a neural network, and explain where it should and should not be trusted.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Data prepared MNIST is not loaded or the pixels are not scaled. MNIST is loaded and the pixels are scaled between 0 and 1. One image is drawn and checked against its label. Network built and trained The model does not compile or train. A Keras network with Flatten, a Dense hidden layer and a 10-neuron softmax output trains with a validation split. Notes how loss and validation accuracy changed across epochs. Test accuracy and predictions No test accuracy, or predictions are not compared with true labels. Reports test accuracy and compares five predictions with the true labels. Also looks at a wrong prediction and suggests why it happened. One change tested No change made, or several things changed at once. One change (more neurons or more epochs), retrained, with a sentence on whether it helped. Also checks the change for signs of overfitting. Limits No limit named, or the limit is wrong. One real limit, such as only knowing centered single digits. Also says how a person would check low-confidence results in real work. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: 10 chances for each of the 5 images
check.why: predict returns a chance for each digit for each image; argmax picks the most likely.

check.q: You want to know if more epochs help. What would you do?
options: Change epochs, neurons and layers all at once
Skip the test set this time
Change only the number of epochs, retrain and compare test accuracy
check.why: Change one thing at a time so you know what caused the difference.
